newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Red Cross signals hope for peace in Colombia.
newsitem.headline: Red Cross signals hope for peace in Colombia.

text.p: The release of 60 Colombian soldiers held by leftist rebels since Aug. 30 should pave the way to talks aimed at ending the country's guerrilla war, the head of the International Committee of the Red Cross said on Thursday.
"The time has come, if it is done with discretion and determination, that an important step will be made," Cornelio Sommaruga told a news conference.

"There is more than simply my optimism (to say) that this will be a serious evolution," he said, referring to how negotiations aimed at winning the soldiers' release could jump-start broader talks between the government and Colombia's largest guerrilla army.
Sommaruga declined to elaborate, but he answered with a curt "I can confirm that" when asked if he thought peace talks were definitely in the offing.

Sommaruga arrived in Bogota on Tuesday for talks with President Ernesto Samper and other senior government and military officials focusing on Colombia's long-running guerrilla conflict and what he described as the need to shore up "respect of fundamental principles of international humanitarian law."
A leading concern of the ICRC are human rights abuses committed by the country's increasingly active and dreaded right-wing paramilitary groups, he said.

"Our concern is to see who is controlling these groups, which are operating close to government forces," Sommaruga said, alluding to frequent allegations of official support for the paramilitaries and right-wing death squads that kill with impunity across much of Colombia.

The Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC), set up as a pro-Soviet force in 1964, seized the 60 soldiers when it overran an army base in a jungle-covered area of southern Colombia nearly nine months ago.

Samper announced on Tuesday that he had ordered the withdrawal of security forces from a 5,000 square mile (13,000 sq km) area of southern Caqueta province for 32 days as part of an agreement with the FARC to win the soldiers' release.
The ICRC is serving as a guarantor of the accord and has dispatched monitors to Caqueta to oversee the demilitarization, which was set to begin at midnight on Thursday.
